title: The Truth About Market Timing (What the Data Shows)
summary: Reviews evidence on market timing: valuations predict returns only weakly, timing strategies underperform in real time, and missing a few best days hurts badly.

assertions.quote: is not reliable enough to provide any meaningful information for investment decision-making

verdicts.note: AQR's out-of-sample tests show valuation-based timing adds little or negative value after 1958.

assertions.quote: have to stay in the market if you want to get the market's returns

verdicts.note: Arithmetically true for every major index, though missing the worst days would help as much; neither is predictable.

assertions.quote: lump sum investing beat dollar cost averaging roughly two thirds of the time

verdicts.note: Vanguard's 2012 study and later replications find lump sum wins about two-thirds of twelve-month periods.

assertions.quote: I do not know of anybody who has done it successfully and consistently

verdicts.note: Mutual-fund and newsletter studies find no persistent timing skill, though it is a strong universal claim.

assertions.quote: You cannot because the world isn't sufficiently regular for people to learn rules.

verdicts.note: Kahneman and Klein's conditions for expertise and forecaster track-record studies support this.
Persistent day traders show no improvement with experience in panel regressions, consistent with short-term trading not being learnable; the feedback mechanism is not tested.

Selling them at that point means that you are betting against momentum, which is a well-documented phenomenon.

verdicts.note: Momentum is one of the most robust return anomalies and valuation signals fire while prices are still rising.
